questions.q: What is the rule for rounding a digit when the number to its right is 4 or less?
questions.a: If the digit to the right is 4 or less, you "round down," meaning the target digit stays the same and all digits to its right become zero. A wrong answer suggests the student confuses "round down" with changing the target digit to a lower value instead of keeping it constant.

questions.q: When rounding 167 to the nearest ten, why do we focus on the number 7?
questions.a: We focus on 7 because it is in the ones place, which determines whether the tens digit (6) stays at 6 or increases to 7. Choosing the wrong digit reveals a misunderstanding of place value positions relative to the target place.

questions.q: Round 342 to the nearest ten and then round 342 to the nearest hundred.
questions.a: Nearest ten: 340 (since 2 < 5). Nearest hundred: 300 (since 4 < 5). An error here shows the student is not identifying the correct "neighbor" digit for different target places.

questions.q: If a stadium holds 855 people, why might rounding to 900 be a better estimate than 800?
questions.a: 855 is closer to 900 than to 800 on the number line, and the rule for rounding 5 is to round up. Students who prefer 800 are ignoring the rule that 5 or more requires rounding up to the next hundred.

questions.q: Is it always better to round to the nearest hundred than the nearest ten? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, it depends on the context; rounding to the nearest ten provides more precision, while rounding to the nearest hundred provides a quicker, rougher estimate. An answer stating "yes" shows the student doesn't understand that precision levels change based on the need for detail.

questions.q: Create a 3-digit number that rounds to 500 when rounded to the nearest hundred, but rounds to 490 when rounded to the nearest ten.
questions.a: A valid answer is 492, 493, or 494. A poor answer (like 501) indicates the student does not understand how rounding to different place values creates different results.
